lessonTitle: Conservative Forces, Potential Energy and Power

blocks.text: At the top of a roller-coaster lift hill the car has almost no speed, yet a minute later it is crossing the valley at over 20 m/s with no engine pushing it. The motor's job is to lift; gravity then hands that height back as speed. When forces return the energy you invest in them, the maths simplifies dramatically.

blocks.markdown: A force is **conservative** if the work it does between two points is independent of the path taken, which is equivalent to saying the work over any closed loop is zero. Gravity and ideal springs are conservative; kinetic friction and drag are not. For a conservative force we can define a **potential energy** $V$ (J) that depends only on position, so that the work done by the force is the decrease in $V$.

blocks.title: Potential energy
blocks.text: Gravitational potential energy is $V_g=mgh$ for height $h$ above a chosen datum ($g=9.81$ m/s$^2$). Elastic potential energy of an ideal spring of stiffness $k$ and extension $x$ from its natural length is $V_e=\tfrac12kx^2$. Only differences in $V$ have physical meaning, so the datum can be chosen freely.

blocks.caption: Conservation of mechanical energy: if only conservative forces (and forces that do no work) act, the sum $T+V$ stays constant. Add the work of non-conservative forces on the left if any are present.

blocks.title: Roller-coaster car
blocks.prompt: A 600 kg car passes a crest 40 m above the base level at 4.0 m/s. Neglecting friction and drag, find its speed at a point 12 m above the base ($g=9.81$ m/s$^2$).

steps.text: Choose the base level as datum. Energy at the crest.
Mass cancels, so work per unit mass: $\tfrac12v_2^2=\tfrac12v_1^2+g(h_1-h_2)$.

blocks.answer: The car's speed at 12 m is about 23.8 m/s, regardless of the track's shape.

blocks.title: Spring-powered launcher
blocks.prompt: A spring gun with stiffness $k=800$ N/m is compressed by 0.12 m and fires a 0.050 kg ball vertically. Neglecting friction, find the height the ball reaches above its compressed position ($g=9.81$ m/s$^2$).

steps.text: Initial energy is elastic, final is gravitational (the ball is momentarily at rest at the top).

blocks.answer: The ball rises about 11.7 m above its starting point.

blocks.markdown: **Is a given force field conservative?** For a force field in the plane, $\mathbf F=F_x(x,y)\,\mathbf i+F_y(x,y)\,\mathbf j$, the force is conservative if and only if the mixed partial derivatives agree: $\partial F_x/\partial y=\partial F_y/\partial x$. If so, a potential function $V(x,y)$ exists with $F_x=-\partial V/\partial x$ and $F_y=-\partial V/\partial y$. If the derivatives differ, the work depends on the path and no potential function exists.

blocks.title: Testing a force field
blocks.prompt: Determine whether $\mathbf F=(6xy+2)\,\mathbf i+(3x^2-2y)\,\mathbf j$ (N, with $x,y$ in m) is conservative, and find a potential function if it is.

steps.text: They are equal, so the field is conservative. Integrate $F_x=-\partial V/\partial x$.

blocks.answer: The field is conservative with potential $V=-3x^2y-2x+y^2$ (J, up to a constant).

blocks.markdown: **Power** is the rate of doing work, measured in watts (W = J/s). For a force $\mathbf F$ acting on a particle moving with velocity $\mathbf v$, $P=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v$. Real machines lose some input power to friction and heat. The **mechanical efficiency** $\eta$ is the ratio of useful output power to input power, $0<\eta<1$. At constant speed up an incline, the net force on the load is zero, so the driving force equals the sum of the downhill weight component and any friction.

blocks.caption: For a load of mass $m$ moved up an incline of angle $\theta$ at constant speed $v$ with kinetic friction coefficient $\mu$.

blocks.title: Power to haul a load up an incline
blocks.prompt: A winch drags a 400 kg crate up a $20^\circ$ incline at a constant 1.2 m/s. The kinetic friction coefficient is 0.25, and the winch's efficiency is 80%. Find the input power ($g=9.81$ m/s$^2$).
blocks.answer: The winch needs about 3.4 kW of input power.

blocks.title: Where conservation of energy fails
blocks.text: $T+V$ is conserved only when all non-conservative forces (friction, drag) do no work. If they do, add their work: $T_1+V_1+U_{nc}=T_2+V_2$ with $U_{nc}$ negative. Do not apply efficiency to the weight component only: it multiplies the whole output power. Always use SI units (W, not kW) in the equation.

points: Conservative forces do path-independent work and have a potential energy; gravity ($mgh$) and springs ($\tfrac12kx^2$) are conservative, friction and drag are not.
With only conservative forces, $T_1+V_1=T_2+V_2$; a planar field is conservative if $\partial F_x/\partial y=\partial F_y/\partial x$.
Power is $P=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v$ and $\eta=P_{out}/P_{in}$; at constant speed up an incline, $F=mg(\sin\theta+\mu\cos\theta)$.

questions.stem: Which statement is true of a conservative force?

options.text: It is always constant in magnitude
It does work only when the particle moves in a straight line
The work it does between two points does not depend on the path

questions.correctOptionText: The work it does between two points does not depend on the path

distractorRationale.a: Springs are conservative but their force changes with extension.
distractorRationale.b: Path shape is irrelevant for conservative forces.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: equivalently, the work over a closed loop is zero.
distractorRationale.d: Work may be positive or negative depending on the displacement direction.

questions.explanation: Path independence is the defining property of a conservative force, and it is equivalent to zero work around any closed path. It allows a potential-energy function to be defined.

questions.stem: A frictionless roller-coaster car starts from rest at the top of a hill and descends a height $h$ along a curved track. Its speed at the bottom

options.text: Depends on the length of the track
Depends on the curvature of the track at the bottom
Depends only on $h$ and $g$, not on the track shape

questions.correctOptionText: Depends only on $h$ and $g$, not on the track shape

distractorRationale.a: Path length does not matter for conservative forces.
distractorRationale.c: Curvature affects the normal force but does no work.

questions.explanation: Gravity is conservative and the normal force does no work, so $\tfrac12mv^2=mgh$ and $v=\sqrt{2gh}$. Neither the track length, its shape nor the car's mass appears.

questions.stem: Which of the following planar force fields (N, with $x,y$ in m) is conservative?
questions.explanation: The test is $\partial F_x/\partial y=\partial F_y/\partial x$. Only $3y\,\mathbf i+3x\,\mathbf j$ passes, with potential $V=-3xy$.

questions.stem: A machine has an efficiency of 0.80 and must deliver a useful output power of 4.0 kW. The input power required is

distractorRationale.d: Adds 20% of the output to 4 kW, which is not the definition.

questions.explanation: Efficiency is $P_{out}/P_{in}$, so the input is $P_{in}=P_{out}/\eta=4.0/0.80=5.0$ kW. The 1.0 kW difference is lost as heat and friction.

questions.stem: A stone is thrown at 12 m/s from the edge of a cliff 20 m above the sea. Neglecting drag and taking $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$, its speed on reaching the sea

options.text: Depends on the angle of the throw
Is about 23.2 m/s, whatever the throw direction

questions.correctOptionText: Is about 23.2 m/s, whatever the throw direction

distractorRationale.a: Adds the speeds 12 and 19.8 instead of the energies.
distractorRationale.b: Speed gained depends only on the height drop, not direction.

questions.explanation: Energy conservation gives $\tfrac12v^2=\tfrac12(12)^2+9.81(20)$, so $v^2=144+392.4=536.4$ and $v=23.2$ m/s. Only the energy matters, so every direction gives the same impact speed.

questions.stem: A 1.5 kg pendulum bob on a 2.0 m string is released from rest with the string at $60^\circ$ to the vertical. Neglecting friction and taking $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$, find its speed at the lowest point in m/s.
questions.explanation: The bob drops by $h=L(1-\cos60^\circ)=1.0$ m. Energy conservation gives $v=\sqrt{2gh}=\sqrt{2(9.81)(1.0)}=4.43$ m/s; the string tension does no work.

questions.stem: A hoist drags a 150 kg crate up a $15^\circ$ ramp at a constant 0.80 m/s. The kinetic friction coefficient is 0.10 and the hoist's overall efficiency is 85%. Taking $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$, find the input power in watts.
questions.explanation: At constant speed $F=mg(\sin15^\circ+0.10\cos15^\circ)=1471.5(0.2588+0.0966)=523.0$ N. The output power is $523.0\times0.80=418.4$ W, so $P_{in}=418.4/0.85=492$ W.

questions.stem: The planar force field $\mathbf F=(c\,xy+2)\,\mathbf i+(3x^2-y)\,\mathbf j$ (N, $x,y$ in m) is known to be conservative. Find the constant $c$, in N/m$^2$.
questions.explanation: For a conservative field $\partial F_x/\partial y=\partial F_y/\partial x$. Here $\partial F_x/\partial y=cx$ and $\partial F_y/\partial x=6x$, so $c=6$ N/m$^2$.

questions.stem: Explain how to test whether a two-dimensional force field is conservative, describe how a potential energy function is obtained when it is, and explain why friction cannot have a potential energy.
markingGuide: Test: $\partial F_x/\partial y=\partial F_y/\partial x$ (zero curl) on a simply connected region.
If true, integrate $F_x=-\partial V/\partial x$ and fix the remaining function of $y$ using $F_y=-\partial V/\partial y$.
Equivalent physical statement: work between two points is path independent and zero over a closed loop.
Friction always opposes motion so its work is negative on every path and increases with path length.
Hence the work depends on the path, so no single-valued potential exists.
questions.explanation: The curl-free condition ensures the line integral is path independent. Friction fails this because going around a closed loop always removes energy.

questions.stem: A motor drives a load up an incline at constant speed. Using the ideas of power and efficiency, explain why the input power is greater than the useful output, state what happens to the difference and show how the driving force relates to the incline angle and friction.
markingGuide: At constant speed the net force is zero, so driving force $F=mg\sin\theta+\mu mg\cos\theta$.
Useful output power $P_{out}=Fv$ (rate at which the load gains potential energy plus rate of friction work).
Difference $P_{in}-P_{out}$ is dissipated as heat in the machine (friction, electrical losses).
Energy accounting: no kinetic energy change at constant speed; weight does negative work at rate $mgv\sin\theta$, friction at rate $\mu mgv\cos\theta$.
questions.explanation: At steady speed the motor force must balance the downhill weight component and friction, so the power is that force times speed. Real machines are not perfect, so the electrical or fuel input must exceed this useful power by the losses.
